title: Monitoring (Basic): Azure Monitor, Alerts, Service Health and Advisor
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain what Azure Monitor collects on its own (platform metrics and the activity log) and what you must switch on (resource logs, guest data and application telemetry).
- Compare metrics and logs, and pick the right one for questions such as "Is the CPU busy?" and "Who stopped this VM?".
- Choose between metric, log search and activity log alerts, and design an action group that reaches the right people.
- Distinguish the Azure status page, Service Health and Resource Health, and use Azure Advisor's five recommendation categories.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Friday, 19:40. A flash sale on batik shirts is in full swing, and the storefront's checkout service still runs on one Azure VM. At 19:52 a customer posts on Instagram: "Website super lambat, checkout gagal terus" — super slow, checkout keeps failing. Forty comments later, at 20:30, someone in marketing forwards you a screenshot. You open the portal: the VM's CPU has been pinned near 100% for forty minutes.

On Saturday morning checkout is down again. This time the VM is simply stopped, and in the team chat everyone, Rizky the contractor included, says "bukan saya" — not me. Pak Budi wonders whether Azure itself had an outage.

On Monday, Ibu Sari has two questions for you: "Why did our customers know before we did? And next time, how quickly can you tell me what happened and who did it?"

Today you design Nusantara Retail's early-warning system — and learn where Azure keeps the evidence.

Reading

1. Azure Monitor: one platform, four questions

When something goes wrong in production, you need fast answers to four questions:

- Is it working? Availability: can customers reach the shop at all?
- Is it working well? Performance: CPU, memory, response times, error rates.
- What changed, and who changed it? Audit: a resize, a stop, a deleted rule.
- Is the problem ours or Azure's? Platform health: an incident in the region, or planned maintenance.

Azure Monitor is the Azure service that collects, stores, analyses and acts on monitoring data. It gathers data from Azure resources, from the operating systems inside your VMs, from your applications and from the subscription itself. There is nothing to deploy for the platform part: every subscription already has it. Alerts, Application Insights, Service Health alerts and many "insights" pages in the portal are all features built on this one platform.

In the portal, everything lives under Monitor: Metrics, Logs, Alerts, the Activity log, Service Health, Workbooks and the insights pages. Most resources also show a slice of the same data in their own menu — a VM's Metrics, Alerts and Activity log pages are simply the Monitor views filtered to that one VM.

The most useful beginner lesson is that some monitoring data is collected automatically and free, while other data must be switched on — and usually costs money once it lands in a workspace.

Data | Collected automatically? | Kept for | Cost to collect
Platform metrics (CPU, network, disk) | Yes, typically every minute | 93 days | No charge
Activity log (control-plane operations) | Yes | 90 days | No charge
Resource logs (operations inside a resource) | No: needs a diagnostic setting | depends on the destination | charged at the destination
Guest OS logs and performance counters | No: needs the Azure Monitor Agent (Lunch 30) | workspace retention | charged per GB ingested
Application telemetry (requests, errors) | No: needs Application Insights | workspace retention | charged per GB ingested

The diagram shows the big picture. Data comes in on the left, lands in one of three stores, and is used on the right.

Tip: Start every investigation with the free data. Open the VM in the portal and look at its Monitoring tab or Metrics: weeks of CPU, disk and network history are already there, without a single setting changed.

2. Metrics and logs: two kinds of evidence

Metrics are numbers measured at regular intervals. Each value has a timestamp and belongs to one resource, and some metrics have dimensions — extra labels such as a disk name or an API name — so you can split a chart. Metrics live in a time-series database built for speed, which makes them ideal for charts and for alerts that must fire within minutes.

Whenever you read a metric you also choose an aggregation over a time grain: Average, Minimum, Maximum, Sum (the portal calls it Total) or Count. The aggregation changes the story. Imagine the storefront VM spikes to 100% CPU for ten seconds every minute and idles in between. Over each minute, the maximum is 100%, the average is about 20% and the minimum is close to zero. All three numbers are correct; they answer different questions.

For a VM, platform metrics such as Percentage CPU, Network In Total and Disk Read Bytes are measured by the Azure host, outside the operating system, so they work even when nothing is installed inside the VM. What the host can't see — free space inside the file system, per-process usage, the system log — needs the Azure Monitor Agent, which you'll meet in Lunch 30. Metrics explorer charts up to 30 days at a time; pan the chart to reach older data within the 93 days.

Logs are records — rows with many columns. A log row might say "GET /checkout returned 500 in 2.3 seconds" or "user dewi@nusantara read the secret db-password". Logs are stored in tables in a Log Analytics workspace and queried with Kusto Query Language (KQL). They are richer than metrics and can answer which, who and why, but you pay for every gigabyte you send and keep, and they usually arrive seconds to minutes after the event.

| Metrics | Logs
Shape | numbers over time | rows with many columns
Example | Percentage CPU = 87 at 19:41 | "GET /checkout returned 500 at 19:41:07"
Freshness | near real time | usually seconds to minutes
Explore with | Metrics explorer | Log Analytics (KQL)
Good question | "Is the CPU high right now?" | "Which requests failed, and why?"
Alert type | metric alert | log search alert
Cost | platform metrics are free | pay per GB ingested and retained

Two special data sources deserve a closer look.

The activity log records every control-plane operation in a subscription: creating, updating, deleting, starting, stopping and resizing resources, assigning roles, and so on. Each entry has a time, an operation, a status, the resource and the caller — the user or service principal that made the request. It also collects Service Health and Resource Health events, alert activations, autoscale actions, Advisor recommendations, Defender for Cloud alerts and Azure Policy actions. The activity log is on by default, free, and kept for 90 days, and its entries can't be edited or deleted, which is exactly why auditors trust it. Read-only operations, such as opening a VM's page, usually aren't recorded. If you need more than 90 days, or want to query it with KQL, export it to a workspace with a diagnostic setting.

Resource logs describe what happens inside a resource — the data plane. Reading a secret from Key Vault, downloading a blob, or running a query in a database are data-plane operations; they never appear in the activity log. Resource logs aren't collected until you create a diagnostic setting on the resource. A diagnostic setting picks the log categories (or a category group such as audit or allLogs) and the destinations: a Log Analytics workspace for querying and alerting, a storage account for cheap long-term archive, Event Hubs for streaming to another tool such as a SIEM, or a supported partner solution. The same setting can also send platform metrics to the workspace, for example to keep them beyond 93 days.

Here is a taste of KQL against the exported activity log. You'll learn the language properly in Lunch 30.

AzureActivity
| where OperationNameValue has "deallocate"
| project TimeGenerated, Caller, ResourceGroup, ActivityStatusValue

Warning: Resource logs are off by default. Teams usually discover this during an incident: the auditor asks who read the database password from Key Vault last Tuesday, and there is nothing to show. Remember the split — the activity log tells you who changed the vault; only resource logs tell you who read the secret. Create diagnostic settings when you create the resource, or let Azure Policy enforce them (Lunches 18 and 31).

3. Alerts: from a signal to someone's phone

An alert rule has four parts:

1. Scope — what to watch: one resource, several resources, a resource group or a subscription.
2. Condition — the signal and the logic, for example "average Percentage CPU greater than 70".
3. Actions — one or more action groups to run when the rule fires.
4. Details — a name, a description and a severity from Sev0 (critical) to Sev4 (verbose).

When the condition is met, Azure Monitor creates an alert — an instance you can see, acknowledge and close on the Alerts page — and runs the attached action groups. Alerts are kept for 30 days. Each alert carries two status fields: the monitor condition (Fired or Resolved), which Azure sets, and the alert state (New, Acknowledged or Closed), which your team sets while it works on the problem.

Alert type | Watches | Typical Nusantara rule | Behaviour
Metric alert | a metric, evaluated every 1–60 minutes | "Average CPU above 70% for 5 minutes" | stateful by default: fires once, resolves itself when the condition clears
Log search alert | the result of a KQL query on a schedule | "More than 5 failed checkouts in 10 minutes" | stateful by default; can be stateless
Activity log alert | new activity log events that match conditions | "A VM in the production group was deallocated" | stateless: fires for every matching event

Service Health and Resource Health alerts are activity log alerts too. You'll also meet smart detection in Application Insights and Prometheus alerts for containers later in the course.

Look closely at a metric alert condition, because most broken alerts are broken here. "Average Percentage CPU greater than 70, window 5 minutes, frequency 1 minute" means: every minute, take the last five minutes of samples, average them, and compare the result with 70. Change one word and the meaning changes:

- Maximum over 5 minutes: "at any moment" — sensitive, and noisy if CPU spikes briefly.
- Average over 5 minutes: "on average" — a sensible default for CPU.
- Minimum over 1 hour: "the whole hour" — so strict that a 15-minute crisis never triggers it.

Longer windows smooth out spikes but react slowly; shorter windows react fast but can flap. If your load has a daily rhythm, dynamic thresholds learn what normal looks like for each hour and alert on unusual values instead of a fixed number.

An action group is a named, reusable list of who to tell and what to run. Notifications include email, SMS, voice calls, push notifications to the Azure mobile app, and email to everyone who holds an Azure Resource Manager role (such as Owner) on the subscription. Actions include webhooks, Azure Functions, Logic Apps, Automation runbooks, Event Hubs and IT service management connectors. One action group can serve many rules. Built-in rate limits protect people from floods: at the time of writing, an email address receives no more than 100 alert emails per hour from a region, and a phone number no more than one SMS every five minutes. Turn on the common alert schema so that every automation receives the same payload shape, whatever the alert type.

Two more tools keep alerting humane. Alert processing rules (once called action rules) change what happens after an alert fires: they can suppress notifications during a planned maintenance window — say, Saturday 01:00–03:00 while Rizky patches the VMs — or add an action group to every alert in a subscription. They don't affect Service Health alerts. And good severity discipline matters: if everything is Sev0, nothing is.

Important: An alert rule without an action group only appears on the Alerts page in the portal — nobody gets an email. Always attach an action group, and point it at a shared mailbox or an on-call rota, not one person who might be on leave.

Good alert rules share four habits. Each one is actionable (whoever receives it knows what to do), carries the right severity, reaches the right audience, and has been tested. The portal's Test action group button sends a sample notification, so you find out that the email lands in a spam folder on a quiet Tuesday, not during an incident.

Platform metrics cost nothing, but alert rules are not all free: metric and log search alert rules carry a small monthly charge per monitored time series or rule, and a subscription can hold at most 100 activity log alert rules. Check the Azure Monitor pricing page before you create hundreds of rules.

4. Is it Azure or is it us? Service Health, Resource Health and Advisor

Azure gives you three views of its own health, from the widest to the narrowest:

- The Azure status page is a public, global view of incidents with widespread impact. It knows nothing about your subscription.
- Service Health is personalised: it reports on the services and regions you use. It shows service issues (incidents happening now), planned maintenance, health advisories (changes that need your action, such as a feature retirement) and security advisories, with updates during an incident and root-cause analyses afterwards.
- Resource Health looks at one resource — this VM, this database — and reports Available, Unavailable, Degraded or Unknown, with a reason (for example platform initiated versus user initiated) and a history.

| Azure status page | Service Health | Resource Health
Scope | all of Azure, all regions | your subscription's services and regions | one resource
Answers | "Is there a big outage?" | "Is an Azure incident or maintenance affecting the services I use?" | "Is this resource healthy, and if not, why?"
Personalised | no | yes | yes
Alerts | no | Service Health alerts | Resource Health alerts
Nusantara example | checking during a famous outage | "Virtual Machines in Southeast Asia: service issue" | "vm-nusa-web: Unavailable, user initiated"

Use them together, from narrow to wide. Start with Resource Health on the broken resource: a user-initiated unavailability points you to the activity log; a platform-initiated one points you to Service Health. Every subscription deserves a Service Health alert — an activity log alert scoped to the subscription, filtered to the regions and services you care about (Southeast Asia and Indonesia Central for Nusantara Retail) and wired to an action group. Add Resource Health alerts for critical resources such as the storefront VM and the orders database.

Azure Advisor is the free consultant in the portal. It analyses your configuration and usage and makes personalised recommendations in five categories:

Category | What it looks for | Nusantara example
Reliability | resilience and continuity risks | "Use availability zones for the storefront VMs"; "enable backup"
Security | weaknesses, surfaced from Microsoft Defender for Cloud | "Close management ports on internet-facing VMs"
Performance | resources that limit speed | a disk or database tier too small for the load
Cost | waste and savings | "Right-size or shut down underused VMs"; reservations for steady workloads
Operational excellence | process and deployment hygiene | "Create Azure Service Health alerts"

You can postpone or dismiss a recommendation with a reason, track progress with the Advisor score, and get alerts when new recommendations appear. Advisor's cost advice feeds Lunch 19, and its security advice is the same list you saw in Defender for Cloud in Lunch 15. One quirk for scripters: the Azure CLI and API still call the reliability category HighAvailability.

5. See it, then bring it together for Nusantara Retail

Data you can't see doesn't help at 20:00 on a Friday. Azure offers several ways to look at it:

- Metrics explorer for quick charts of one or more metrics, which you can pin to an Azure dashboard.
- Workbooks — interactive reports that mix text, metric charts and log queries, with parameters such as "pick a VM".
- Azure Monitor dashboards with Grafana, built into the portal at no extra cost, and Azure Managed Grafana, a paid service for teams that also need non-Azure data sources, Grafana alerting or scheduled reports.
- Insights — ready-made experiences such as VM insights and Application Insights.

Application Insights deserves a first look today, because the Friday problem was really an application problem. It is Azure Monitor's application performance monitoring feature: it records every request to the storefront, how long it took, whether it failed, which dependencies (the database, the payment API) it called, and which exceptions were thrown. It can also run availability tests that call your site from several locations around the world. New Application Insights resources store their data in a Log Analytics workspace, and you add them with autoinstrumentation or the OpenTelemetry libraries. Lunch 30 goes deep.

Here is the starter kit you'll propose to Ibu Sari:

1. An action group, ag-nusa-oncall, that emails the IT on-call mailbox and texts the duty phone.
2. A metric alert on the storefront VM: average CPU above 70% for five minutes, Sev 2.
3. An activity log alert: any VM in the production resource group deallocated or deleted, Sev 1.
4. A Service Health alert for incidents and maintenance in the regions Nusantara Retail uses.
5. A Resource Health alert for the storefront VM.
6. Diagnostic settings on Key Vault and the orders database, so "who read what" is answerable.
7. Ten minutes every Monday with Advisor.

With this in place, the next Friday story changes. The duty phone buzzes about five minutes after CPU starts to climb, long before Instagram notices. On Saturday, the activity log names the person who stopped the VM, Resource Health labels it user initiated, and Service Health confirms that Azure was fine. That's the answer to Ibu Sari's two questions: you'll know first, and you'll know why.

Pause and think: At 02:10 Resource Health shows the storefront VM as Unavailable — user initiated, and Service Health shows no incident in Southeast Asia. Where do you look next to find out who did it, and which alert type would have woken you at 02:01 instead of 08:00?

Going deeper: Lunch 30 · Monitoring (Advanced) (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/lunches/30-monitoring-advanced.html) covers Log Analytics workspace design, the Azure Monitor Agent, KQL and Application Insights in depth.

Field notes from Stefanus

An alert is a promise that someone will act. Before I create an alert rule, I write its description as an instruction to the person who will read it at night: what it means, the first thing to check, and when to escalate. If I can't write that sentence, the rule isn't ready, or it belongs on a dashboard instead of in someone's inbox. Once a month, before they age out of the Alerts page, I go through every alert that fired: each one that nobody acted on is retuned, given a lower severity, or deleted. An inbox full of ignored alerts is worse than an empty one, because it teaches the team to stop reading. And I never trust an action group until I have tested it end to end, on the phone of whoever is actually on call.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: Overview of Azure Monitor alerts (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/alerts-overview) — alert types, stateful versus stateless alerts, and how rules, processing rules and action groups fit together.
- Microsoft Learn: Activity log in Azure Monitor (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/fundamentals/activity-log) — what is recorded, how long it's kept, and how to export it to a workspace.
- Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Service Health? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/service-health/overview) — Azure status, Service Health and Resource Health side by side.
- Microsoft Learn: Introduction to Azure Advisor (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/advisor/advisor-overview) — the five recommendation categories and how to act on them.

quiz.q: Dewi wants an email within a few minutes whenever the storefront VM's CPU stays above 80% for five minutes. Which alert type should she create, and with which aggregation?
quiz.a: A metric alert on Percentage CPU with the Average aggregation over a 5-minute window. Why: platform metrics arrive automatically every minute, so a metric alert reacts quickly without any agent or workspace.

quiz.q: On Saturday the storefront VM was stopped and deallocated. Ibu Sari wants the name of the person who did it before lunch. Where do you look?
quiz.a: In the activity log (Administrative category): filter on the operation Deallocate Virtual Machine and read the Caller field. Why: every control-plane operation is recorded automatically, with its caller, for 90 days.

quiz.q: An auditor asks which users downloaded invoice PDFs from Blob storage last week. The storage account has existed for a year with default settings. Can you answer?
quiz.a: No. Downloads are data-plane operations, recorded only in resource logs, and resource logs are collected only after you create a diagnostic setting. Create one now so the question can be answered next time. Why: the activity log covers control-plane changes, not reads of the data.

quiz.q: Rizky created an alert: "Minimum Percentage CPU greater than 70 over 1 hour". During a 15-minute flash-sale spike the CPU sat at 100%, yet the alert never fired. Why, and what is a better condition?
quiz.a: Minimum over one hour only triggers if CPU stays above 70% for the entire hour, so a 15-minute spike can never satisfy it. Use Average over 5 minutes (evaluated every minute). Why: the aggregation and window define what "high" means.

quiz.q: The storefront VM is unreachable. Resource Health says Unavailable — platform initiated, and Service Health shows an active service issue for Virtual Machines in Southeast Asia. Whose problem is it, and what should you do?
quiz.a: It's an Azure platform problem, not a change your team made. Follow the incident updates in Service Health, apply your recovery plan (Lunch 17), and make sure a Service Health alert exists so you hear about the next one first. Why: platform-initiated unavailability plus an active regional issue points to Azure, not to your configuration.

takeaways: Platform metrics and the activity log are collected automatically and free; resource logs, guest OS data and application telemetry must be switched on and are charged where they land.
Metrics answer "how much, right now?" quickly and cheaply; logs answer "what, which, who and why?" with KQL.
An alert rule is scope + condition + action group + severity — the aggregation and window decide whether it ever fires, and the action group decides whether anyone hears it.

The activity log tells you who changed what; Resource Health tells you whether one resource is healthy and why; Service Health tells you about Azure incidents and maintenance in your services and regions.
Azure Advisor gives free, personalised recommendations in five categories — reliability, security, performance, cost and operational excellence — so make reviewing them a habit.

lab.title: Know before customers do
lab.text:
What you'll build

Last Friday Nusantara Retail's customers noticed a slow shop before anyone at head office did, and on Saturday nobody could say who had stopped the storefront VM. In this lab you build the early-warning system that fixes both problems. setup.sh gives you a small storefront VM. You add an action group that emails you, a CPU metric alert, an activity log alert that catches a deallocated VM, and a Service Health alert for your subscription. Then you make the CPU sweat on purpose and receive the alert, answer "who did it?" from the activity log, ask Advisor for advice, and repair a colleague's alert rule that never fires.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)).
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install.
- An email address you can read on your phone during the lab (a personal address is fine).
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/16-monitoring-basic
source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 16)
export ALERT_EMAIL="you@example.com"     # change this to your own address

- Create the starting point — one small Linux VM with no inbound ports open. It takes about 3–5 minutes:

bash setup.sh

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist. Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway.

Tip: Cloud Shell disconnects after about 20 minutes without typing. If that happens, reconnect and reload the variables:

cd ~/azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/16-monitoring-basic && source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 16); export ALERT_EMAIL="you@example.com"
VM_ID=$(az vm show -g "$RG" -n vm-nusa-web --query id -o tsv)
AG_ID=$(az monitor action-group show -g "$RG" -n ag-nusa-oncall --query id -o tsv 2>/dev/null)

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–7 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · See what Azure already collects

Before you build anything, look at the data you get for free: platform metrics and the activity log. No agent, no workspace, no settings.

VM_ID=$(az vm show --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-nusa-web --query id --output tsv)

# Which CPU metrics does a VM publish?
az monitor metrics list-definitions --resource "$VM_ID" \
  --query "[?contains(name.value, 'CPU')].{metric:name.value, unit:unit, aggregation:primaryAggregationType}" \
  --output table

# The last hour of CPU in 5-minute buckets
az monitor metrics list --resource "$VM_ID" --metric "Percentage CPU" \
  --interval PT5M --aggregation Average Maximum \
  --query "value[0].timeseries[0].data[].{time:timeStamp, avg:average, max:maximum}" \
  --output table

# Who created the VM? The activity log already knows.
az monitor activity-log list --resource-group "$RG" --offset 2h \
  --query "[?operationName.value=='Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write'].{time:eventTimestamp, caller:caller, status:status.value}" \
  --output table

You'll notice metrics such as CPU Credits Remaining: $VM_SIZE_SMALL is a burstable B-series size, which can run at full speed only while it has CPU credits. A new VM starts with enough credits for this lab.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Open the VM, then Monitoring › Metrics and pick Percentage CPU; switch the aggregation between Avg and Max and watch the line change. Then open Activity log in the VM's menu.

Checkpoint: you see Percentage CPU in the definitions, a column of low CPU values (the VM is idle), and one or more activity log rows for virtualMachines/write with your account as the caller.

Task 2 · Create an action group that emails you

An action group is the "who to tell" list. One group can serve many alert rules, so you create it first.

az monitor action-group create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name ag-nusa-oncall \
  --short-name nusaoncall \
  --action email oncall-email "$ALERT_EMAIL" usecommonalertschema \
  --output none

AG_ID=$(az monitor action-group show --resource-group "$RG" --name ag-nusa-oncall --query id --output tsv)

az monitor action-group show --resource-group "$RG" --name ag-nusa-oncall \
  --query "{enabled:enabled, shortName:groupShortName, receivers:emailReceivers[].{name:name, status:status, commonSchema:useCommonAlertSchema}}" \
  --output yaml

- --short-name (up to 12 characters) appears in SMS messages.
- --action email <receiver-name> <address> usecommonalertschema adds one email receiver that uses the common alert schema.
- Alert emails come from Microsoft no-reply addresses (for example azure-noreply@microsoft.com). If you use a work mailbox with strict filters, add that sender to your safe list.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Monitor › Alerts › Action groups › Create. After saving, open the group and select Test action group to send yourself a sample email — the best way to discover spam-folder problems early.

Checkpoint: enabled: true and one receiver named oncall-email with status Enabled.

Task 3 · Create the CPU metric alert

Now the rule: "every minute, average the last five minutes of CPU; if it's above 70%, fire a Sev 2 alert and run the action group".

az monitor metrics alert create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name alert-cpu-high \
  --scopes "$VM_ID" \
  --condition "avg Percentage CPU > 70" \
  --window-size 5m \
  --evaluation-frequency 1m \
  --severity 2 \
  --action "$AG_ID" \
  --description "Storefront VM: average CPU above 70% for 5 minutes" \
  --output none

az monitor metrics alert show --resource-group "$RG" --name alert-cpu-high \
  --query "{enabled:enabled, severity:severity, window:windowSize, every:evaluationFrequency, metric:criteria.allOf[0].metricName, aggregation:criteria.allOf[0].timeAggregation, operator:criteria.allOf[0].operator, threshold:criteria.allOf[0].threshold, autoResolve:autoMitigate}" \
  --output yaml

Flag | Meaning
--condition "avg Percentage CPU > 70" | aggregation (avg), metric name, operator and threshold
--window-size 5m | the lookback period: how much data each evaluation looks at
--evaluation-frequency 1m | how often the rule runs
--severity 2 | Sev 0 is critical, Sev 4 is verbose
--action "$AG_ID" | which action group to run when it fires

Tip: Prefer the portal? VM › Alerts › Create › Alert rule. Signal Percentage CPU, threshold Static, aggregation Average, operator Greater than, value 70, check every 1 minute, lookback period 5 minutes. Pick ag-nusa-oncall on the Actions tab.

Checkpoint: the output shows enabled: true, window: PT5M, every: PT1M, aggregation: Average, operator: GreaterThan and threshold: 70.0.

Task 4 · Make the CPU sweat and catch the alert

Time to test the alarm. You'll run a tiny script inside the VM with Run Command — no SSH, no open ports, no packages installed. Take a look at it first:

cat cpu-load.sh

It starts one busy loop per vCPU, wrapped in timeout, so the load stops by itself. Start 15 minutes of load:

az vm run-command invoke \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name vm-nusa-web \
  --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts @cpu-load.sh \
  --parameters 15 \
  --query "value[0].message" --output tsv

Run Command takes 20–60 seconds to return. Then watch the CPU climb (run it again every couple of minutes):

az monitor metrics list --resource "$VM_ID" --metric "Percentage CPU" \
  --interval PT1M --offset 20m --aggregation Average \
  --query "value[0].timeseries[0].data[].{time:timeStamp, avg:average}" \
  --output table

Expect CPU near 100% within two or three minutes, and the alert email about 5–10 minutes after you started the load. While you wait, re-read section 3 of the lunch, or open Monitor › Alerts in the portal and filter on your resource group to watch the alert appear.

When the email has arrived, you can stop the load early instead of waiting for the timer:

az vm run-command invoke --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-nusa-web --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts @cpu-load.sh --parameters stop --query "value[0].message" --output tsv

A few minutes after CPU drops, the rule resolves itself and sends a second, "Resolved" email — metric alerts are stateful.

Tip: Prefer the portal? VM › Operations › Run command › RunShellScript, paste the contents of cpu-load.sh and replace ${1:-10} with the number of minutes. The output appears in the portal when the script returns.

Checkpoint: an email from Azure Monitor mentioning alert-cpu-high and Sev 2 is in your inbox, and the alert appears under Monitor › Alerts with monitor condition Fired (later Resolved).

Task 5 · Hear about Azure's problems: a Service Health alert

Service Health alerts tell you when Azure publishes an incident, planned maintenance or an advisory that affects the services you use. The rule is an activity log alert. It is stored in your lab resource group (so the clean-up removes it) but its scope is the whole subscription.

SUB_ID=$(az account show --query id --output tsv)

az monitor activity-log alert create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name alert-service-health \
  --scope "/subscriptions/$SUB_ID" \
  --condition category=ServiceHealth \
  --action-group "$AG_ID" \
  --description "Azure service issues, planned maintenance and advisories for this subscription" \
  --output none

az monitor activity-log alert show --resource-group "$RG" --name alert-service-health \
  --query "{enabled:enabled, location:location, scope:scopes[0], condition:condition.allOf}" --output yaml

Don't expect an email today: it fires only when Azure publishes a Service Health event that affects you.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Service Health › Health alerts › Create service health alert lets you tick the services, regions and event types (service issue, planned maintenance, health advisory, security advisory) instead of listening to everything. That's what you'd do in production.

Checkpoint: enabled: true, location: Global, the scope is /subscriptions/<your-subscription-id> and the condition contains category equals ServiceHealth.

Task 6 · "Who stopped the shop?" — an activity log alert and a query

First the alarm: an activity log alert that fires whenever a VM in this resource group is deallocated.

RG_ID=$(az group show --name "$RG" --query id --output tsv)

az monitor activity-log alert create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name alert-vm-deallocated \
  --scope "$RG_ID" \
  --condition "category=Administrative and operationName=Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/deallocate/action and status=Succeeded" \
  --action-group "$AG_ID" \
  --description "A VM in this resource group was deallocated" \
  --output none

Now play Rizky and stop the VM. This also stops the compute meter, which is good for your budget:

az vm deallocate --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-nusa-web

Then answer Ibu Sari's question from the activity log. New entries can take a few minutes to appear, so repeat the command if the table is empty:

az monitor activity-log list --resource-group "$RG" --offset 1h \
  --query "[?operationName.value=='Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/deallocate/action'].{time:eventTimestamp, caller:caller, status:status.value}" \
  --output table

The alert email usually arrives within a few minutes; activity log alerts can take up to about 20 minutes.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Monitor › Activity log, filter on the resource group and the operation Deallocate Virtual Machine, and open an entry: the Summary shows Event initiated by. Then open the VM's Help › Resource health: it shows the VM as unavailable because a user stopped it — "us", not Azure.

Checkpoint: the table lists the deallocate operation with your account as the caller and a Succeeded row, and an email for alert-vm-deallocated arrives.

Task 7 · Ask Advisor for a second opinion

Advisor reviews your subscription for free. List its recommendations, then filter by category:

az advisor recommendation list \
  --query "[].{category:category, impact:impact, problem:shortDescription.problem, resource:impactedValue}" \
  --output table

az advisor recommendation list --category Cost --output table

The CLI's categories are HighAvailability (shown as Reliability in the portal), Security, Performance, Cost and OperationalExcellence. Advisor analyses resources periodically, so a brand-new VM may take up to a day to get recommendations; what you see now may concern other resources in your subscription, or the list may be empty.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Search for Advisor. The overview shows the five categories and your Advisor score. Open a recommendation to see the affected resources and the Postpone and Dismiss options.

Checkpoint: the command runs without errors. Note one recommendation (if any) and its category. An empty list is a valid result in a fresh subscription.

Break it and fix it

Rizky copied the CPU alert for the operations team, "with fewer false alarms". Create his rule exactly as he did:

az monitor metrics alert create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name alert-cpu-rizky \
  --scopes "$VM_ID" \
  --condition "min Percentage CPU > 70" \
  --window-size 1h \
  --evaluation-frequency 15m \
  --severity 3 \
  --action "$AG_ID" \
  --description "Rizky's CPU alert" \
  --output none

Symptom: during a 15-minute flash sale at 100% CPU, alert-cpu-high fires but alert-cpu-rizky never does. You don't need to run the load again to prove it: look at what each rule would have seen during your Task 4 spike.

# Hourly view: what Rizky's rule evaluates
az monitor metrics list --resource "$VM_ID" --metric "Percentage CPU" \
  --interval PT1H --offset 3h --aggregation Minimum Average Maximum \
  --query "value[0].timeseries[0].data[].{hour:timeStamp, min:minimum, avg:average, max:maximum}" \
  --output table

# 5-minute view: the windows where the good rule saw an average above 70
az monitor metrics list --resource "$VM_ID" --metric "Percentage CPU" \
  --interval PT5M --offset 3h --aggregation Average \
  --query "value[0].timeseries[0].data[?average > \`70\`].{time:timeStamp, avg:average}" \
  --output table

Hint: why does it never fire, and how do you fix it?

Two choices make the rule blind:

- Minimum means "the lowest value in the window". For the minimum to exceed 70, the CPU must stay above 70% for the entire window.
- A one-hour window means the whole hour. Your spike lasted 15 minutes, so the hourly minimum stayed low (look at the min column) — even the hourly average stayed far below 70.

You can't switch the aggregation of an existing condition with a simple flag, so replace the rule (or simply delete it: alert-cpu-high already covers this case, and duplicate rules mean duplicate emails):

az monitor metrics alert delete --resource-group "$RG" --name alert-cpu-rizky

az monitor metrics alert create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name alert-cpu-rizky \
  --scopes "$VM_ID" \
  --condition "avg Percentage CPU > 70" \
  --window-size 5m \
  --evaluation-frequency 1m \
  --severity 3 \
  --action "$AG_ID" \
  --description "Rizky's CPU alert, fixed: average over 5 minutes" \
  --output none

Want proof? Start the VM (az vm start -g "$RG" -n vm-nusa-web), run Task 4's load again for 10 minutes, and watch both rules fire. Deallocate the VM again afterwards.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. Set ALERT_EMAIL before running it to also check the receiver's address.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This deletes resource group rg-lunch16-<suffix> and everything in it: the VM, its disk, network interface, public IP, network security group and virtual network, the action group and all four alert rules — including the Service Health alert, which lives in the resource group even though it watches the subscription. Nothing is created outside the resource group. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes. Fired alerts stay visible for up to 30 days and activity log entries for 90 days; they cost nothing.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
(ResourceGroupNotFound) Resource group 'rg-lunch16-…' could not be found. | setup.sh hasn't run, or this Cloud Shell has a different random suffix | run bash setup.sh; check the suffix with cat ~/.azlunches-suffix
No alert email 15 minutes after starting the load | the email is in a spam folder, the receiver was unsubscribed, or CPU never passed 70% | check junk mail; run the Task 2 show command — if the receiver's status isn't Enabled, run az monitor action-group enable-receiver --resource-group "$RG" --action-group-name ag-nusa-oncall --name oncall-email; check the CPU values from Task 4
CPU stays around 10–20% while the load runs | the burstable VM has used its CPU credits and is held at its baseline | check the CPU Credits Remaining metric; stop the load, wait, and try a shorter run — or use a larger size by setting VM_SIZE_SMALL before setup.sh
(Conflict) Run command extension execution is in progress. Please wait for completion before invoking a run command. | Run Command runs one script at a time | wait a minute and try again
Run Command runs for minutes and returns nothing | the VM is still booting, or it can't reach Azure over HTTPS to return the output | wait two minutes after creating or starting the VM; make sure the VM still has its public IP (it provides outbound access)
The deallocate alert hasn't arrived after 10 minutes | activity log events can take up to about 20 minutes to reach alerting | wait, then check the rule's condition with the Task 6 query and az monitor activity-log alert show
az advisor recommendation list prints nothing | Advisor hasn't analysed the new resources yet | that's normal; try az advisor recommendation list --refresh or look again tomorrow in the portal
An error about the combination of window size and frequency | some lookback and frequency combinations aren't allowed | use the values in this guide (5 minutes and 1 minute)

Stretch goals

- Resource Health alert: create an activity log alert with --condition category=ResourceHealth and --scope "$VM_ID", then deallocate and start the VM and compare the email with the Task 6 one.
- Quiet hours: in Monitor › Alerts › Alert processing rules, create a rule that suppresses notifications for your resource group during a weekly maintenance window, and test it with Task 4.
- Dynamic threshold: create a second CPU rule with --condition "avg Percentage CPU > dynamic medium 2 of 4" and read how Azure learns the normal pattern.
- SMS: add an SMS receiver with az monitor action-group update --add-action sms … (check that your country is supported first).
- Longer memory: export the activity log to a Log Analytics workspace (Monitor › Activity log › Export Activity Logs) and query the AzureActivity table — a preview of Lunch 30.
- A one-page view: pin the CPU chart to an Azure dashboard, or open Monitor › Dashboards with Grafana and explore the prebuilt VM dashboard.

Challenge brief

Run bash setup.sh to get resource group rg-lunch16-<suffix> with the VM vm-nusa-web. Then build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep), in that resource group:

1. An action group named ag-nusa-oncall with at least one email receiver.
2. A metric alert named alert-cpu-high on vm-nusa-web: Average Percentage CPU greater than 70 over a 5-minute window, enabled, wired to the action group.
3. An activity log alert named alert-service-health, stored in the resource group, scoped to your whole subscription, for the ServiceHealth category, wired to the action group.
4. An activity log alert named alert-vm-deallocated that fires when a VM in the resource group is deallocated, wired to the action group.
5. Prove it works: receive the CPU alert email under load, and the deallocate email after stopping the VM.
6. If you create Rizky's rule (alert-cpu-rizky), make it use the Average aggregation and a window of 15 minutes or less — or delete it.

Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? Peek at solution.sh or switch to Guided mode.
